title: Tacx Nera Smart Trainer In-Depth Review: Consistently Inconsistent
content:
﻿

The Tacx Nera smart trainer is the first newly released smart trainer in a number of years from Garmin-Tacx, following the Tacx NEO 3M back in 2023. The Tacx Nera is meant to act as a viable sub-$1,000 Tacx smart trainer option, after the company has largely left that market (no, the near-decade-old Flux trainers in the backroom don’t count). The question is, can Garmin stick the landing here?

The new Nera adds virtually all of the capabilities that are now commonplace, including built-in WiFi – but also expands upon ones that are available, introducing a movement fore/aft/lateral system that moves more than other trainers with simple cushioned feet (but not quite as much as the Tacx Motion Plates). Plus, it has support for Zwift Virtual Shifting/Zwift Cog, the Zwift Ride Back, as well as support for all other smart trainer apps on the market.

Both my wife and I have been putting it through its paces over the last three+ weeks, across many hours of trainer rides, to figure out where it works well, and where it falls short. Rush out this review, I did not. But after all this testing, I’m left rather puzzled. Let’s get into it!

What’s New & Specs:

It’s a tiny bit tricky to write a ‘What’s New’ section when Tacx hasn’t released a new mid-range trainer for the better part of a decade. For real. The last attempt was the Tacx Flux 2 in 2018, though they did quietly tweak some internals in 2020, but didn’t officially launch that as a new trainer. Either way, that’s a silly-long time ago.

– Added omnidirectional moving feet/balls for increased movement
– Added built-in WiFi
– Added built-in 11sp cassette (11-28) or Zwift Cog V2
– Added a handle
– Added heart rate sensor bridging
– Added Zwift Ride compatibility
– Added Zwift Protocol compatibility
– Added Zwift Race compatibility
– Increased Max Incline to 20%
– Increased Max Wattage to 2,200w
– Increased accuracy claim to +/- 1%
– Added support for Tacx Alpine gradient simulator

As a funny aside, a lot of people might not realize/remember this, but prior to the Tacx NEO 3M era, Tacx actually didn’t ship cassettes with any of their trainers. Wahoo started that trend way-back-when they launched the original KICKR V1, but it would take nearly a decade for Tacx to follow along. Even the Tacx NEO 2T in 2019 didn’t come with a cassette.

In any case, here’s the rest of the leftover specs. Or rather, just all the specs:

– Direct drive trainer: This means you remove your rear wheel
– Flywheel: It has a flywheel weight of 13.51lbs (6.13 kg)
– Cassette: Equipped with either Zwift COG or 11-speed cassette (also compatible with 9-12 speed cassettes – some cassette types will require an adapter)
– Sound: Very quiet, though not quite as silent as some units.
– Handle: Yes!
– Flexible Feet for Motion/Sway: Yes, all directions
– Protocol Compatibility: ANT+ FE-C, ANT+ Power, Bluetooth Smart Trainer Control, Bluetooth Smart Power (everything you need), Direct Connect WiFi, Zwift Protocol
– WiFi: Yes, built-in, Direct Connect to all apps via WiFi
– Zwift Race Mode: Yes, 10 Hz
– Heart Rate Bridging: Yes, can rebroadcast your heart rate sensor within a single channel, ideal for Apple TV Zwift users (who are Bluetooth channel limited), as well as some Zwift controller bridging compatibility.
– App Compatibility: Anything and everything
– Skewer Compatibility: All the skewers and adapters you could ask for: Road 130mm, 135mm, 142x12mm, 148x12mm, also other adapters available.
– Zwift Ride Frame Compatible: Yes
– TACX Alpine Grade Simulator Compatible: Yes
– Max Incline: 20% simulated grade
– Max Wattage: 2,200 watts resistance
– Claimed Accuracy: +/1.0%
– Max Rider Weight: 264lbs/120kg
– Unit/Trainer Weight: 54.5 lbs (24.7kg)
– Power Cable Required: Yes, power block compatible with 100-240v
– Pricing: $999USD

As you can see, the specs are essentially the same as you’d see from the Wahoo KICKR V6, and slightly higher than mid-range trainers like the Wahoo KICKR CORE V2 (which have 16% simulated grade). Though inversely, the ride feel/movement on the Tacx NERA is better/more than the Wahoo KICKR V6 (but not as much as the now discontinued Wahoo KICKR MOVE, or the still available Tacx NEO 3M).

Finally, note that the Tacx NERA manual currently lists a ‘Max Bike Weight’ value. That weight actually has nothing to do with physical bike weight limitations, but rather the software setting that can be tweaked within the app to simulate the bike’s weight plus your weight on climbs/gradients. Tacx is updating the manual shortly to reduce confusion (otherwise that weight would be less than the Zwift Frame weight).

Got all that? Good, let’s get this unboxed.

In the Box & Setup:

The Tacx Nera is a very simple trainer to set up and get going. At least, assuming you’ve got an 11-speed bike for the 11-speed cassette, or assuming you bought the Zwift Cog version and plan to use Zwift.

To begin, you’ve got the box above, and then here’s what’s inside once you lay it all out:

Inside that zip baggie are the thru-axle adapters and quick-release skewer, plus that blue thingy is for removing the entire freehub if you need to switch to a different freehub (which would require buying an accessory). For example, if you wanted to put on a 12-speed XDR cassette from SRAM. Whereas a Shimano 12-speed cassette wouldn’t require that switch.

In any case, setting up the trainer is silly easy. You’re basically just putting four bolts into the trainer. Two per leg, it’s stupid simple:

The entire process takes about 1-2 minutes, depending on your IKEA skill set.

After that, you’ll connect up the power cable. Note that there’s no secondary power brick here; it’s all included inside the internals of the unit, which I appreciate. Though be aware it’s not quite like the same power cable you’ve seen in the past (the kind you might plug into a computer). Instead, it’s got this little three-hole connector:

This is still an IEC standard cable, though- technically an IEC C5 cable. So if you want to buy a longer one, just search on Amazon for IEC C5, and you’ll find all sorts of lengths of that cable.

Ok, with that done, we’re ready to roll. Note there’s no configuration or tweaking of the feet/moving platform bits. They are what they are. I kinda like that though, as I’m sorta tired of dealing with tweaking a bunch of feet/legs to be the right angles/lengths/etc.

Daily Usage:

First up is getting your bike on the trainer. As with all direct drive trainers, you’ll remove the rear wheel of the bike, and then put the chain directly on the trainer cassette or cog. If you’re using the Zwift Cog variant, it’s easiest to shift into the middle of the cassette before placing it on the trainer, so everything lines up nicely.

One thing I’m a bit surprised by is just how tight the clearance is on most of our bikes (on the non-drive side). We’re talking barely 1mm of clearance in most cases, to the case itself. This is largely because Tacx shrouds the flywheel with a case (likely for safety reasons), whereas Wahoo and others have an exposed flywheel design. While all of our bikes do ultimately fit (including triathlon, road, and gravel), it’s still astonishingly tight/close:

In any case, if using the Zwift Cog edition, you’ll probably want to tweak the adjustment ring on the Zwift Cog. This adjusts the left/right position of the Zwift Cog itself. You can usually just look straight down and see if it’s perfectly aligned. If it’s making any weird noises, it’s probably not aligned. Simply rotate that little piece until things are visually spot-on.

Also, as a reminder, there’s no electronic technology whatsoever within the Zwift COG itself. It’s literally the equivalent of two kid IKEA bowls with a single cog (from a cassette) in the middle:

Instead, the virtual shifting piece happens entirely from the handlebars with the Zwift Clicks, which control shifting between Zwift and the trainer. Thus, if you have the Zwift COG, now is a good time to install those Clicks. There are a few different places you can stick them, which is entirely user preference. Generally speaking, the ‘best’ place is on the inside or outside of your handlebars, like so:

Alternatively, you can place them on the outside of the shifters too. As I noted in my Zwift Click V2 Review, overall these are great, though I find the bands absolutely suck (mostly from a taking on/off standpoint). Instead, I prefer to use the extra rubber bands that come with Garmin bike computers. You can buy a package of them here.

Now of course, if your Tacx Nera is the cassette version, then none of this actually matters, because you’ll shift with your bike’s shifters. That said, you don’t actually have to have the Zwift Cog to use Zwift Virtual shifting (the Clicks), you can use that just fine with any cassette, including the one on the Tacx Nera.

Speaking of that cassette, in my case, because I found it annoying that they included an 11-speed cassette, I swapped it to a 12-speed cassette. All of our bikes are 12-speed (save the gravel bikes, which are 13-speed).

Now, with all that sorted, I do want to note that you can connect to the Tacx App to configure the Tacx Nera settings. This includes bits like the rider weight (which improves the simulation feel), as well as the Race Mode and WiFi settings. All of this is straightforward.

I will point out that as part of this entire thing, anytime you want to connect to the trainer via Bluetooth, you have to press the side button to enter Bluetooth pairing mode. The entire “connecting app to your trainer” thing can only be described as dumpster-fire annoying. Most of the time it won’t connect (either for me or DesFit, also reviewing his unit 5,000 miles away), or requires pressing the button every time you want to connect. And then on top of that, stats like hours ridden and distance ridden are simply wrong. The kilometers have been all over the map (some rides it updates, some rides it doesn’t), and even the total hours are notably short at this point.

According to Tacx, it shouldn’t always require a button press for existing pairings, but it sounds like they’re tracking down some bugs that are causing this to require the button press more often than it should. Again, no other trainer requires all this level of annoyance. I haven’t figured out if this is a Garmin lawyer problem (trying to comply with EU RED regulations), or a Garmin engineering problem (trying to be “more secure”). I don’t know.

Further, if you want to configure heart rate bridging, you can do this in the Tacx App as well. This took a bit of finagling to get working properly with the Garmin HRM-600 for reasons that aren’t clear to me. But eventually I got it happy. I suspect it’s due to the secure BT pairing process/state on the HRM-600.

Now, with all that sorted, I’m just gonna open up Zwift to make this section simple. Later on in the review, I cover other apps. Here in Zwift, we can see the pairing screen and what things look like. You’ll see both the Bluetooth connection/signal, as well as the WiFi one (if configured). And had I also put an ANT+ stick in my computer, I’d see that connection type too. You can also see the bridged HR sensor here too:

Once that’s done, you’ll start riding. The trainer will automatically control the resistance based on what the app is sending. When it comes to smart trainers, there are essentially two core modes that you’ll be riding in most of the time:

ERG Mode: Setting a specific power level – i.e., 185w. In this mode, no matter what gearing you use, the trainer will simply stay at 185w (or whatever you set it to).

Simulation (SIM) Mode: Simulating a specific outdoor grade – i.e., 7% incline. In this mode, it’s just like outdoors in that you can change your gearing to make it easier or harder. Wattage is not hard-set, only incline levels. For a Tacx Nera configured with the Zwift Cog, this mode will *ONLY* officially work with Zwift and Rouvy, via the Zwift Click. Other apps work, but it’s unofficial and might be inconsistent. Whereas with a regular cassette, this works in any app. TLDR: If you plan to use other apps, just get the mechanical cassette version. You can always buy a Zwift Cog later and swap it out.

In the case of simulation (aka slope) mode, the Tacx NERA can simulate from 0% to 20% incline – the same as the Wahoo KICKR V6. Both of which are more than most of the $400-$500 trainers that do 16%-18%. To be really clear here, you don’t actually want to ride your bike at that gradient. Nobody does. Not in real life, and not in your living room.

The point being, there are lots of good reasons to get a higher-end bike trainer (such as ride feel). But I wouldn’t let the maximum simulated gradient be one of those reasons, unless you’re one of the handful of people who really want that difference between 16% and 20%. The vast majority of climbs in most cycling apps top out in the 12-13% range. Sure, there are a few moments that might briefly touch 16%, but almost no training apps have routes that regularly go beyond that.

And atop that, most apps, Zwift included, have a ‘Trainer Difficulty’ level, which reduces the app-dictated gradient further. In Zwift’s case, that setting is by default configured at 50%. That means that a 20% grade climb ‘feels’ like 10%. This won’t impact your in-game speed (since that’s based on wattage), but it does impact how the climb feels to your legs, and which specific gearing you’ll use.

That said, all of my testing with the Tacx Nera is at 100%. I simply don’t understand the logic of buying a fancy trainer to simulate the outdoors only to get rid of the hills. If that’s the case, just go ride routes in the Netherlands. But hey, that’s me.

(Yes, I know Zwift and other platform racers like to reduce this setting to 20-25% to make racing more efficient, but you don’t even want to get me started on that fiasco…)

In any case, if you’ve got a mechanical cassette, you’ll shift just like you normally would. But if you’ve got the Zwift Cog you’ll shift with the Zwift Click (or buttons on the Zwift Ride Frame). In that case, you can configure your Zwift shifting to simulate one of a few different virtual drivetrains. One option is a continuous 24-speed virtual drivetrain (with 24 gears). The other is more akin to regular 2x bikes with multiple front chainrings (e.g., big ring and little ring), and you can then see this within the Zwift HUD at the left side (e.g., Gear 1-4):

With the Click V2, you can also configure it in a 2x configuration (two virtual chainrings up front), which is what I prefer, allowing me to shift similar to SRAM-style shifting. You can change this in the menu as well:

Anyway, moving along, one of the big factors that folks look at when comparing trainers is inertial feel – or basically, road feel. Does it feel right/correct when accelerating, or sprinting, or just simply pedaling along. Obviously, this is somewhat subjective. I’ve rotated through the KICKR CORE 2, Tacx NEO 3M, and Tacx NERA, literally side-by-side (while troubleshooting accuracy issues), moving a bike between them. The NEO 3M clearly has better road feel, but the CORE 2 and Nera don’t feel all that different to me in most scenarios. This, of course, is logical given both have fairly similar flywheel weights (though equally, flywheel weight is only one factor, because differences in the internal gearing of the belt can easily double the effective flywheel inertia).

As for the sounds of the trainer, it’s actually not as quiet as the KICKR CORE 2. I can’t quite tell if that’s electronic components inside, or just the whirring of the flywheel noise echoing inside the NERA case. Either way, whatever fan you use will definitely be louder than the trainer, so don’t overthink this. Same goes for any shifting noises, all louder than the trainer itself.

Which then finally gets us to the movement aspect of things. On the underside of the Tacx Nera are what are actually five balls that allow for forward/aft/side movement. The concept of using balls (inflated or tennis balls) in homegrown trainer platforms has been around for years. It’s just that more recently, the big companies have refined this concept a bit more.

With the Tacx Nera, this allows for fore/aft/tilting movement, naturally. The idea here (just like most movement) is to provide just enough movement so that it feels slightly more natural than riding a concrete fence. And the Tacx Nera accomplishes that well. It’s not as much movement as the Tacx NEO 3M’s forward/back movement, but equally, if you locked that out (because you felt it was too much), this would feel better. And this feels better than any Wahoo KICKR/CORE/etc. variants. It’s well done.

Of course, this probably goes without saying, but if you only ride the Zwift Ride frame, then of course you’re not going to get as much movement (specifically, virtually no forward/aft movement), because the front of that frame is a flat surface, rather than the wheel of your bike rolling slightly forward/backwards. I dive into this more in the Zwift Cog/Frame section, but I do want to at least point that out, as I’ve seen some weird things out there around that.

App Compatibility:

The Tacx Nera smart trainer supports all of the industry standards and proprietary protocols used by smart trainers today. This includes ANT+, Bluetooth Smart, WiFi, and more. This is somewhat notable as we’ve seen both Elite & Decathlon (Van Rysel) remove ANT+ on some recent smart trainers. I don’t have a specific issue with that per se in 2026, but for those that want ANT+ for older compatibility, it’s there. Meanwhile, for proprietary protocols like the Zwift Protocol, it supports that too.

The Tacx Nera smart trainer supports all the following technical standards:

ANT+ FE-C Control: This is for controlling the trainer via ANT+ from apps and head units, and includes power, speed, & cadence data.

ANT+ Power Meter Profile: This broadcasts as a standard ANT+ power meter, with cadence and speed data baked in.

Bluetooth Smart FTMS: This is the industry standard for apps controlling the trainer via Bluetooth Smart, and includes ANT+ power and cadence baked in. Additionally, with heart rate bridging, it’ll include that data too.

Bluetooth Smart Power Meter Profile: This broadcasts as a standard Bluetooth Smart power meter, with cadence and speed data baked in.

Wireless (WiFi) Direct Connect: This uses WiFi built-in, to apps on the same WiFi network, this includes power/speed/cadence/heart rate data, along with trainer control. Additionally, with heart rate bridging, it’ll include that data too.

Zwift Protocol: This is the control protocol that Zwift uses to support Virtual Shifting, and other Zwift-specific features. This is used between the trainer and Zwift, to control the trainers resistance.

From a connectivity standpoint, it supports unlimited ANT+ connections, and supports three (3) concurrent Bluetooth connections. The three Bluetooth connections are useful if you have a watch (such as an Apple/Polar/Suunto/COROS Watch) that connects to the trainer to read your power data for training load/recovery, and then you’ve got the Zwift app reading your data; this ensures that even if your phone is still randomly paired to the trainer behind the scenes, it doesn’t block any connections.

Additionally, as outlined in the earlier section, it supports bridging of sensor connections via the trainer, including heart rate.

Notably, I did ask about whether Garmin/Tacx plans to support OpenBikeControl, which is an emerging open standard that essentially allows for better openness than the Zwift Protocol. They noted that they are looking at it (especially after the Stages SB200 launch included it), and in fact, Garmin’s TrainingPeaks Virtual already supports it. But while Tacx is looking at it, OpenBikeControl today is more for indoor smart bikes than indoor trainers (since it focuses specifically on the button controller elements).

In any case, the Tacx Nera supports so-called ‘Race Mode’, which means that it transmits your power data at a much higher rate than once/second. In Race Mode, it transmits at 10hz (10 times a second), when connected via WiFi or Bluetooth.

Now, when it comes to my testing of the Tacx Nera, I’ve been using it with tons of apps, mostly as part of my testing for an upcoming Trainer App review. Thus far, I’ve used the Tacx Nera with:

– Rouvy (regular cassette and SIM mode)
– TrainerRoad (ERG mode)
– Zwift (SIM & ERG mode, both Zwift COG & regular cassette)
– TrainingPeaks Virtual (regular cassette and SIM mode)
– MyWhoosh (ERG mode, with a bit of SIM mode)
– BikeTerra (SIM mode)
– Vieta (SIM mode)
– RideCave (SIM mode)

I’m continuing to ride other apps, but that’s just where I stand as of this publishing.

Across all of these apps, I didn’t have any issues with control or usage. I’ve used the Tacx Alpine with a number of them, including most recently in the past few days, Zwift, BikeTerra, and Vieta.

Again, stay tuned to the site for a follow-up with more trainer apps included in a larger trainer app guide that I’m working on.

Zwift Cog & Zwift Ride:

I do want to briefly note that the unit supports the Zwift Ride trainer, as well as, of course, the Zwift Cog. In my case, I installed the Zwift Cog manually (since the unit shipped with the 11sp cassette). Note that if shipped with the Zwift Cog, it includes the 18-tooth version (18t) also used on Elite trainers, not the 14t version that’s used on Wahoo trainers.

In the initial firmware of the Tacx Nera at launch, there were issues where, with the Zwift Cog (or really any cassette) in Zwift specifically, the virtual shifting feel was substantially off. After DesFit and I reported these issues to Tacx, they did some digging and found a firmware bug that resulted in one of the values for how it handles the braking action, causing the issues we saw. In a newly released firmware, this seems much improved.

Next, when used with the Zwift Ride, the one thing to remember is the Zwift Ride has a perfectly flat front foot, so you won’t get much of the forward/back movement, because the Zwift Ride nullifies that (in the same way it’d nullify it on a Wahoo KICKR MOVE trainer).

Thus, when looking at reviews of the movement aspect of the Tacx Nera trainer, you need to ensure the review is actually showing it being used with a real bike, not just the Zwift Ride. The reality is the overwhelming majority of indoor training cyclists are not currently riding the Zwift Ride, so it only makes sense to test a movement-focused trainer with a real bike for the majority of my testing.

You’ll still get the side-to-side (leaning) movement with the Zwift Ride, in fact, it arguably leans even more because of the extra weight. Though, it doesn’t react as fast because of said extra weight. Further, you just won’t get much in the way of front/back movement unless you put your Zwift Ride front leg on a skateboard or other rolling device (which definitely isn’t recommended by Garmin/Tacx/Zwift, but hey, that never stopped most of us from doing dumb things on our bikes). And finally, keep in mind that the Zwift Ride frame weighs some 38 lbs (17.4 kg), which will further dampen the movement feeling.

Tacx Alpine Compatibility:

I just wanted to briefly note in here somewhere that the Tacx Nera is fully compatible with the Tacx Alpine, which is Tacx’s gradient simulator. That is to say, the Tacx Alpine will raise and lower the front end of your bike, mimicking the up/down motion of a climb or descent. The Alpine can simulate a gradient of +25% up, and -10% down.

The way this works is that the Alpine technically talks to the trainer (Nera in this case), which in turn means it’s compatible with any app out there. Said differently, rather than the apps talking to the Alpine (and having to have special coding for that), the app simply sends the gradient to the trainer like normal (e.g. 7%), and then the trainer instantly tells Alpine what to do. It all works perfectly fine.

Obviously you can check out my full Tacx Alpine review for more details on how that all works, but I figured I’d at least include a mention here. Note that the Tacx Nera won’t get to 3rd-party gradient simulators, such as the Wahoo KICKR CLIMB, since each of these different gradient simulators only talks to trainers in its own brand (technically Elite’s Rizer is compatible with others, but in reality it’s not a great experience).

Trainer/Power Accuracy:

As a rule of thumb, smart trainer (or power meter) accuracy testing falls into one of two camps:

Camp 1: Everything just works, perfectly every ride, and my reviewing life is simple
Camp 2: Everything goes wrong, all at once, except when it doesn’t, and you’re left with endless useless data sets trying to figure out whether it’s the thing you’re testing that went wrong, or the reference units.

My head hurts.

I’m solidly in Camp 2, and sometimes it’s the other power meter, and sometimes it’s the Tacx Nera. But after nearly a month of creating data sets and troubleshooting, a good chunk of the time it’s the Tacx Nera that’s problematic. The bigger issue is that it’s inconsistent. Some days/rides it’s fine, some days/rides it’s all over the map.

Initially, I thought I was dealing with just a pair of Favero pedals that were being finicky, and indeed, that was certainly the case for some early sets (I’d swap the bike to a Wahoo KICKR CORE 2 and Tacx NEO 3M next to the Tacx Nera and the Favero pedals would still be off). So mark one brief win to the Tacx Nera.

Then I changed to another set of power meter pedals (Rally x10). In fact, I even went as far as before every single ride I’d jump on one of those two, usually the Tacx NEO 3M because it’s widely considered the most accurate out there, and do a validation that the pedals were happy that day. Here’s what that looks like:

You can see here the Rally pedals being about 3w higher than the trainer. That makes total sense based on drivetrain losses. As a general rule, I’d consider anywhere in the 2-5w range normal for drivetrain losses/accuracy differences between that 200-400w level. We could have an academic debate about whether that’s 2w or 4w or whatever. It’d involve beer, a bunch of engineering geeks, and nobody would really care at the end of it. Point being, the pedals should *ALWAYS* be higher than the trainer, because you ‘lose’ power as it transfers from your foot through the pedal, through the crankset, through the drivetrain, and eventually into the trainer via the cassette.

Sometimes companies will calibrate their trainers to match that of a power meter pedal/crankset. But that’s not what I’ve heard from Tacx.

First, let’s look at a TrainerRoad ERG mode ride. In this case, I had ridden the trainer at midday (my unit is technically outside), where it was about 72°F/22°C. Then, 8-9 hours later that evening, it had dropped down to 55°F/12°C. In this case, I purposefully did not do any warm-up riding to see what it does. I did half a rotation of my crank arm to wake it up, and then boom, off I went riding. Here are the results:

At the beginning, you can see straight away that the Tacx Nera is some 13 watts low (on a mere 156w). That’s stupid-too-low. But, having gotten off a conference call with Tacx about this, they said at the time that it could take 4-8 minutes to warm up. And perhaps one spin-down. So, I gave it that, and then fast-forward to the 8-minute marker;

And above, you can see things did settle down. It was now within 1-3w. Though slightly variable. One second it was higher than the pedals, and a few seconds later below the pedals. It wasn’t 13w offset anymore, but it wasn’t stable either. Still, you could vaguely write that off to +/-1% on each unit. I guess.

Fast forward to the end of the workout, and now we’re offset by some 10w again in some cases:

Fuuuuuuuuddddddddggeee.

Welcome to hell. Where I’ve been the last nearly four weeks of trying to figure this out. And keep in mind I’m only showing you a fraction of the data sets, so that you won’t fall asleep. Each one of these represents a real-life ride of getting out there and sweating through it all. Plus all the other outside rides/runs I’m doing for other reviews.

Here’s another example from a few days prior to that, a Zwift video route ride. Here’s the high level compared to Favero. You’ll notice those big gaps there; that’s where I’m troubleshooting and doing zero offsets (calibrations) after seeing weird things.

If we take a look at that point around the 10-minute marker, you can see me take a poke at it, and here the offset is some 20-30w. Less than ideal.

So back to another spin down and calibration I go. And following that, things seem reasonably close. The pedals are a few watts higher than the Tacx Nera, as they should be.

Still, at this juncture I’m unconvinced on where the issue is. These are early days in my Nera accuracy time warp.

You see, in talking to Tacx about the issue, they noted that they expect to see some drift in the first 4-8 minutes. Not actually because of temperature issues inside the case or anything else. In fact, they note that they have a real temp sensor directly measuring the flywheel, updating every second, to handle exactly this (most trainers use a proxy of some sort for temp compensation). Instead, they noted the drift is actually more mechanical in nature, as the belt warms up. Hence the 4-8 minutes. Further, they said the first 10-15 minutes of the very first ride on the trainer from the factory, it might be off. But then in talking to other reviewers, they said anywhere from 3-5 rides of up to an hour each, before things settled. Either way, I’m *WELL* past that at this point, somewhere closer to 20 hours of riding between my wife and I.

When it comes to that continuous calibration to handle temperature shifts, they noted that anytime you stop pedaling and the trainer spins down (even for a few seconds in a sprint), it’ll continuously calibrate. Effectively the same as other trainers do in the market. There is no manual spin-down option here. It’s just always doing it.

And in some rare scenarios, I can actually see these shifts taking place where something is off, and I’ll just stop pedaling for 5-7 seconds, and then start pedaling again and boom, it’s good. Here, let me show you an example of that.

This simulation mode ride in Vieta, we start off and see the Tacx Nera is about 8w low on 170w (which is too much in my opinion). You can see I’m repeatedly stopping (coasting) to see if any shifts happen in those first 20 minutes.

Here we are 14 minutes later; before I do another one, it’s still offset by 7 W:

In short, that doesn’t finally happen until a shift at the 14-minute marker, when things ‘snap’ into place, and the power is now identical. Of course, it shouldn’t be identical. It should be that 2-5w lower than the pedals. Debate as you see fit, but now we’ve essentially shifted the power by 8w, instantly.

But by the end of the ride, the Tacx Nera would creep up even more, now 2-4w *OVER* the pedals.

Next, we’ve got a Zwift ride on Titans Grove, one of my usual testing loops. Here, we can see things start off 10w offset:

And even some 18 minutes in, it’s still offset. Sometimes, for a few seconds it’ll match, but it drifts back to 8-10w offset.

Sure, by the end of the ride, some 40 minutes later, it is finally where it should be.

And on and on I’d go. A TrainerRoad workout that starts off the first 10 minutes off, but then simmers out correctly:

Or a BikeTerra ride I did, again, starts off 8-10w low, but simmers out as well around the 10-15 minute marker and was fine the rest of the way.

Or this RideCave climb I did, which remained non-stop offset at 10w almost the entire time. Except finally at the very end I did some hard pushes going downhill and let it coast briefly. Then, and only then, did it snap to reality. Nearly an hour later.

But you know how you solve it? Have someone else warm it up first. Here on November 12th, I had my wife ride for an hour first:

Then, I swapped my bike on within perhaps 2-3 minutes and started riding. Here is an ERG/structured workout on MyWhoosh, and it’s spot on from start to end.

I rest my case.

Look, a $1,000 trainer shouldn’t require you to deploy a warm-up buddy to get it ready for you to ride. Nor should it be off 10w for the first 10-15 minutes of every ride. Nor should it require you to randomly stop/start the ride to ‘coast’ and get the calibration values right. It should just work.

If $400-$500 trainers can do this, then so can a $1,000 unit. The Wahoo KICKR CORE 2, Elite Rivo, and JetBlack Victory can all be accurate from the start, every ride. It’s just that simple.

I’ve spent a lot of time going back and forth with Tacx on all assortment of Tacx Nera issues. And for everything that’s not-accuracy related, they’ve made tons of quick fixes since launch to address those issues. But for all accuracy-related issues, the simple gist of it has been explaining how it works. There’s no real concern or urgency about the accuracy inconsistencies that I and others are seeing. I’ve been around the Garmin/Tacx boat long enough to know when they are legit concerned about an issue that I stumble into, versus more of a “that is what it is”. This, to me, implies this is an engineering/design decision, not an issue with my specific unit. Or, anyone else’s units.

Wrap-Up:

A couple of years back, I asked someone at Garmin/Tacx why they hadn’t made a new mid-range smart trainer yet, and they commented that Garmin is really good at making products and making the best or most premium hardware in a given category. That’s something they understand how to do well, as history easily shows us. But they noted that Garmin often struggles when they try to compete in a price-crowded landscape. Not struggle in terms of product quality, but struggle to find the right balance of features vs. price (vs. undercutting their own premium offerings).

If we momentarily set aside the accuracy issues, Garmin’s challenge with the Tacx Nera is that the smart trainer pricing floor has essentially disappeared underneath them. Not due to some ‘race for the bottom’ (because the $399-$499 smart trainers are really effing good), but because they’ve become a bit of a commodity. Garmin knew this, and it’s largely why they sat out 6-8 years’ worth of smart trainer advancements in that price category. The Wahoo KICKR V6 is a benchmark trainer at $849 (and now on sale for $679). Sure, it has slightly less movement than the Tacx Nera, but not some crazy amount that makes it worth $320 more.

But more than that, the Tacx Nera simply has real-world accuracy issues. One can call it drift, and that’s certainly true (and Tacx even agrees with that), but equally, drift issues are simply accuracy issues by another name. And based on my interactions with Tacx thus far, it doesn’t seem like they’re really that concerned with the accuracy issues that myself and others are seeing (which is different than other issues I’ve seen that they quickly fixed). I’ve spent a lot of time testing, re-testing, and re-testing against multiple power meters, multiple riders, many apps, switching back and forth to the NEO 3M, and even more re-testing. It’s simply consistently inconsistent. This wasn’t just riding it 2-3 times and calling it a review. I’ve gone back and forth with the Tacx engineers on it too, and again, the answer when it comes to accuracy/drift seems to be: That’s how this trainer works.

Sure, anytime you talk about Garmin/Tacx products, you have the Tacx Tax. That ‘tax’ covers lots of things, such as generally better support than their competitors, sometimes better build/accuracy quality (like the Tacx NEO 3M), and all assortment of other random things. But in the case of the Tacx Nera, those premium things don’t really matter if the base product itself simply isn’t accurate.

Thus, until those issues are addressed, it’s nearly impossible to recommend the Nera.
